title: Can and can't
seoTitle: Can and can't in Turkish: -abil and -ama
intro: This unit adds **can**: *Yüzebilir misin?* (Can you swim?), *Maalesef gelemem* (Sorry, I can't come). It covers the ability suffix `-(y)Abil`, its negative `-(y)AmA`, what the two are used for (ability, permission, possibility and polite requests), and the words *hiç*, *kimse* and *hiçbir şey*, which go with a negative verb.

blocks.text: **Can** is a suffix that goes between the stem and the tense: `-(y)Abil`. It comes from *bilmek* (to know), and it is usually followed by the aorist *-ir* of [unit 4](gp-aorist-forms) and the type I endings: *gel-* + *-ebil* + *-ir* + *-im* → *gelebilirim* (I can come).

**Harmony.** Only the first vowel of `-Abil` follows the stem: *-ebil* after e, i, ö, ü; *-abil* after a, ı, o, u. *Bil* always keeps its i, so everything after it is front, even after a back stem: *yapabilirsin*, *okuyabiliriz*. And the aorist after *bil* is always *-ir*, as *bilmek* is one of the thirteen.

**Buffer y and stem changes.** After a vowel, a y comes in: *oku-* → *okuyabilir*, *bekle-* → *bekleyebilir*. The four verbs you know from the future change in the same way: *diyebilir*, *yiyebilir*, *gidebilir*, *edebilir*.

rows.en: he, she or it can come

blocks.title: *yapmak* (to do): a back stem, but front endings after *bil*

blocks.text: **Questions.** As in every tense with type I endings, the ending moves onto `mI`, which follows *bil*: *Gelebilir misin?* (Can you come?), *Yapabilir misiniz?* For **they**: *Gelebilirler mi?*

**With other tenses.** `-(y)Abil` can carry any tense. With `-(I)yor` it describes an ability you have now, often one you have just acquired; with `-DI` it says you managed to do something; with `-(y)AcAk` it looks ahead.

items.en: My brother can play the guitar.
I can speak a little Turkish now.
In the end we managed to find tickets.
Will you be able to come tomorrow?

blocks.text: *Bil* never changes its vowel: *yapabilirim*, not *yapabılırım*; *okuyabilir*, not *okuyabılır*. And the aorist after it is always *-ir*: *gelebilir*, never *gelebiler*.

French splits **can** between pouvoir and savoir (je sais nager, I can swim). Turkish uses `-(y)Abil` for both, although for a language it often just says *bilmek*: *Türkçe biliyorum* (I know Turkish).

The negative of `-(y)Abil` is not *-ebilme*. It is a short `-(y)A`, the same a or e as in *-abil* and *-ebil*, followed by the negative `-mA`, with no *bil*: *gel-* + *-e* + *-me* + *-m* → *gelemem* (I can't come). After it comes any tense.

blocks.text: In the aorist, the inability form takes the endings of the negative aorist ([unit 4](gp-aorist-negative)): *-m* for **I**, *-yIz* for **we**, `-z` with the others. Before `-(I)yor`, the a or e of `-mA` narrows as usual: *gelemiyorum*, *yapamıyorum*, like *gelmiyorum*.
**Questions** follow each tense: *Gelemez misin?* (Can't you come?), *Gelemedin mi?* (Couldn't you come?). *Gelemez misiniz?* is also a gentle request: **couldn't you come?**

items.en: I couldn't sleep at all last night.
Ali won't be able to go to work tomorrow.

blocks.text: Three negatives to keep apart: *gelmem* (I don't come, I won't come: a choice), *gelemem* (I can't come) and *gelmeyebilirim* (I may not come, in the next section).
*Anlayamadım* (I couldn't understand, I didn't catch that) is a polite way to ask someone to say something again: *Pardon, anlayamadım.*
`-(y)Abil` does the work of English **can**, **could** and **may**.

items: **Ability**: *Yüzebilir misin?* (Can you swim?), *Ece gitar çalabilir* (Ece can play the guitar).

**Permission**: *Girebilir miyim?* (May I come in?), *Buraya oturabilir miyim?* (Can I sit here?), *Gidebilirsin* (You can go, you may go). Refusing permission uses **can't**: *Burada sigara içemezsiniz* (You can't smoke here).
**Possibility**: *Yağmur yağabilir* (It may rain), *Elif geç kalabilir* (Elif may be late). **May not** is `-mA` + y + `-Abil`: *Gelmeyebilir* (He may not come).
**Polite requests**: *Tuzu verebilir misiniz?* (Could you pass the salt?), *Bana yardım edebilir misin?* (Could you help me?).

blocks.caption: Asking for the salt, from direct to polite

English
rows: Could you pass the salt, please?

items.en: It may rain in the evening.

blocks.text: *Gelemez* and *gelmeyebilir* look alike but say different things: **he can't come** and **he may not come**. In the second one, `-mA` comes before *-ebil*, which stays whole.
*Olabilir* (it's possible, could be) is a common answer on its own: *Ali hasta mı? — Olabilir.* (Is Ali ill? — Could be.)

sections.title: Nobody, nothing, never: hiç and kimse

blocks.text: Some words need a negative verb, and Turkish then keeps both negatives: *Kimse gelmedi*, literally **nobody didn't come**, means **nobody came**. Without the negative the sentence is wrong: never *Kimse geldi*.

*Hiçbir* is written as one word, and the noun after it takes its case as usual: *Hiçbir şeyi unutmadım* (I didn't forget anything), *Hiç kimseyi görmedim* (I didn't see anyone), *Hiçbir yere gitmiyorum* (I'm not going anywhere).

**In questions** these words lose their negative sense: *hiç* means **ever** and *kimse* **anyone**: *Hiç Kapadokya'ya gittin mi?* (Have you ever been to Cappadocia?), *Evde kimse var mı?* (Is anybody home?). *Biri* and *bir şey* work in questions too: *Bir şey ister misin?* (Would you like something?)

items.en: Have you ever watched oil wrestling?

blocks.text: With a past verb, *hiç* means **ever** in a question and **never (so far)** in a negative answer: *Hiç Türkiye'ye gittin mi? — Hayır, hiç gitmedim.* (Have you ever been to Turkey? — No, I've never been.)
*Hiç* can stand alone as an answer: *Ne yaptın? — Hiç.* (What did you do? — Nothing much.) In a full sentence it needs the negative verb: *Hiçbir şey yapmadım.*
French works the same way: personne n'est venu, je n'ai rien compris. Standard English uses one negative: **nobody came**, **I understood nothing** or **I didn't understand anything**.

summary: **Can**: stem + `-(y)Abil` + *-ir* + type I ending: *gelebilirim*, *yapabilirsin*, *okuyabilir*. *Bil* never changes.
Questions move the ending onto `mI`: *Gelebilir misin?* Other tenses: *gelebiliyorum*, *gelebildim*, *gelebileceğim*.
`-(y)Abil` gives ability (*Yüzebilirim*), permission (*Girebilir miyim?*), possibility (*Yağmur yağabilir*) and polite requests (*Tuzu verebilir misiniz?*).
*Kimse*, *hiç kimse*, *hiçbir şey* and *hiç* need a negative verb: *Kimse gelmedi*. In questions they mean **anyone**, **anything**, **ever**: *Hiç gittin mi?*
